summary: Decide whether one person can attend every meeting, i.e. no two intervals overlap (touching ends are fine).
mainInsight: Sort by start time. If any two meetings overlap, then some pair of neighbours in sorted order overlaps, so it is enough to check each meeting's start against the previous meeting's end.
invariant: After checking meeting i, meetings 0..i in sorted order are pairwise non-overlapping.

approaches.name: Sort by start, compare neighbours
approaches.spaceComplexity: O(1) to O(n) for the sort

commonMistakes: Using <= instead of <, so meetings that touch at time t are wrongly reported as overlapping.
Failing on an empty list (0 meetings is allowed).

cards.answer: Sort the intervals by start time and check each one against the previous end. Clue: The question is whether any two meeting intervals overlap, and the input intervals are not given in order.
keyPoints: The question is whether any two meeting intervals overlap, and the input intervals are not given in order.
cards.explanation: Overlap questions on intervals become a neighbour check once the intervals are sorted by start.

promptVariants: After sorting by start, why is checking neighbours enough?
Why can't two non-adjacent meetings overlap while every neighbour pair is fine?
options: If i and j > i + 1 overlap, so do i + 1 and i
Sorted intervals can never overlap at all
Every meeting has the same length after sorting
Only the first and last meeting can overlap
cards.answer: If i and j > i + 1 overlap, so do i + 1 and i
cards.explanation: Meeting i + 1 starts no later than j, so if j starts before i ends, so does i + 1. Any overlap shows up between some neighbours.

promptVariants: Three back-to-back meetings [1,5], [5,8], [8,9]: can one person attend all?
options: false, two meetings share a time
cards.explanation: A meeting ending at t and one starting at t do not overlap, so the check must be start < previous end, not <=.

incorrectOptionExplanations.false, two meetings share a time: Sharing the boundary time is not an overlap here.
incorrectOptionExplanations.true only if sorted first: The answer does not depend on input order; sorting is just how we check.

promptVariants: Your loop starts with curEnd = 0 and special-cases i == 0. Is that needed?
What do the `i == 0` check and curEnd = 0 do in this solution?
cards.answer: Since starts are >= 0, curEnd = 0 already lets the first meeting through, so `i == 0` is redundant. Looping from 1 and comparing with intervals[i - 1][1] removes both the special case and the extra variable.
keyPoints: curEnd = 0 already admits the first meeting
Compare with the previous interval's end directly
cards.explanation: Removing special cases is part of writing interview-clean code.

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the canonical code?
Derive the running time of sort plus neighbour scan.
cards.explanation: The sort dominates; the scan is linear.

promptVariants: Apart from the sort's own memory, the scan uses O(___) space.

cards.explanation: Only a loop index; Timsort may use O(n) auxiliary space.
